---
title: "Colours and palettes"
description: "Every dial's measured colours, its eight-colour discrete palette and its sequential ramp."
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  dev = "ragg_png",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.4,
  out.width = "100%"
)
library(ggplot2)
library(bauhaus)
```

## Where the colours come from

Each dial of the screensaver is a small colour system. Its colours were measured from the dial
artwork and are stored in `bauhaus_dials`:

* **paper** and **plate**: the plate as shown on screen (lifted by 13/255) and its nominal colour.
* **numeral**: the hour numerals.
* **track**: the minute track and the minute numerals.
* **steel**, **hand** and **hub**: the polished steel of the indices, hands and hub.
* **lume** and **lume_hand**: the luminous paint in the indices and hands, by daylight.
* **shadow_core**, **shadow_ambient** and **shadow_contact**: the tinted shadows under the hands
  and indices. On coloured dials these are deep, saturated versions of the plate.

The palettes are built from these:

* The **discrete** palette has eight colours. It opens with the dial's own signature colour and ink,
  then borrows accents from the other dials (their plates, inks and shadow tints), chosen to stand
  out against this dial's plate. Apart from the dial's own inks on the two mid-tone plates, Signal
  Blue and Tennis, the first six colours of every palette reach a contrast ratio of at least 3:1
  against the paper.
* The **sequential** palette is a ramp of the dial's own colours. On light dials it runs from the
  daylight lume through the signature colour to the numeral ink; on dark dials it rises from just
  above the plate through the track ink to the numeral ink.

## All palettes

```{r overview, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 9}
d <- bauhaus_dials
n <- nrow(d)
rows <- data.frame(dial = d$name, y = rev(seq_len(n)), paper = d$paper, ink = d$numeral)

dots <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  data.frame(y = rows$y[i], x = 3 + 0:7 * 0.62, colour = bauhaus_palette(d$dial[i]))
}))

ggplot() +
  geom_tile(aes(x = 5.65, y = y, fill = I(paper)), data = rows, width = 11.3, height = 0.94) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.15, y = y, label = dial, colour = I(ink)), data = rows, hjust = 0, size = 3.4, family = bauhaus_font_family("semibold")) +
  geom_point(aes(x, y, colour = I(colour)), data = dots, size = 5.2) +
  lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    ramp <- bauhaus_palette(d$dial[i], type = "sequential", n = 200)
    annotation_raster(matrix(ramp, nrow = 1), xmin = 8.3, xmax = 10.7, ymin = rows$y[i] - 0.21, ymax = rows$y[i] + 0.21)
  }) +
  annotate("text", x = c(3 + 3.5 * 0.62, 9.5), y = n + 0.85, label = c("Discrete", "Sequential"), size = 3.2, family = bauhaus_font_family(), colour = "#004F5D") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 11.3), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, n + 1.2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_grain(fill = bauhaus_colours("turquoise")[["paper"]], colour = NA, sigma = 3.8))
```

## The colours of each dial

```{r table, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
swatch <- function(hex) sprintf('<span class="swatch" style="background:%s"></span><code>%s</code>', hex, hex)
cols <- c("paper", "numeral", "track", "steel", "lume", "shadow_core")
cat("<table class='table'>\n<thead><tr><th>Dial</th>", paste0("<th>", cols, "</th>", collapse = ""), "<th>Discrete palette</th></tr></thead>\n<tbody>\n")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(bauhaus_dials))) {
  row <- bauhaus_dials[i, ]
  pal <- paste(sprintf('<span class="swatch" style="background:%s" title="%s"></span>', bauhaus_palette(row$dial), bauhaus_palette(row$dial)), collapse = "")
  cat(sprintf(
    "<tr><td><strong>%s</strong><br><code>\"%s\"</code></td>%s<td style='white-space:nowrap'>%s</td></tr>\n",
    row$name, row$dial, paste0("<td>", vapply(cols, function(c) swatch(row[[c]]), ""), "</td>", collapse = ""), pal
  ))
}
cat("</tbody></table>\n")
```

Get any of them in R:

```{r colours}
bauhaus_colours("signal_blue")
bauhaus_palette("signal_blue")
bauhaus_palette("signal_blue", type = "sequential", n = 5)
```

## Using the palettes

Inside a Bauhaus theme the dial's palettes are already the defaults. Scales let you use another
dial's palette, reverse it, or bin it:

```{r reverse}
ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_bauhaus_c("sky_blue", reverse = TRUE) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Reversed sequential palette", x = "Waiting (min)", y = "Eruption (min)") +
  theme_bauhaus("sky_blue")
```

```{r binned}
ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, z = density)) +
  geom_contour_filled(bins = 7) +
  scale_fill_bauhaus_d("salmon") +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Filled contours", x = "Waiting (min)", y = "Eruption (min)", fill = "Density") +
  theme_bauhaus("cream")
```

They work with other themes as well:

```{r other-theme}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_bauhaus_d("turquoise") +
  labs(title = "A Bauhaus palette on theme_minimal()", x = "Displacement (l)", y = "Highway mpg") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The discrete palettes stop at eight colours, because more categories than that are hard to tell
apart. With more groups, ggplot2 warns and leaves the extra ones grey; consider lumping the smallest
groups together.

For base graphics, use the colour vectors directly:

```{r base}
op <- par(bg = bauhaus_colours("yellow")[["paper"]], family = "sans")
barplot(VADeaths, beside = TRUE, col = bauhaus_palette("yellow", n = 5), border = NA)
par(op)
```
